public_rationale: On the plain reading, the question is whether OpenAI had fixed hallucinations by March 2024. It had not. OpenAI's own GPT-4 page says the model 'still is not fully reliable (it “hallucinates” facts and makes reasoning errors)' and calls hallucination 'still a real issue'. A Stanford study published in January 2024 tested OpenAI's GPT-3.5 among other models and found hallucination rates of 69% to 88% on specific legal queries. OpenAI did report reducing hallucinations relative to earlier models. That cuts against reading 'categorically' as 'no progress at all', but not against the plain claim that OpenAI had failed to fix the problem.
limitations: The independent study covers GPT-3.5 and the legal domain, not GPT-4 in general.
'Categorically' is read as 'has not fixed'. Real reductions were reported.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: OpenAI has failed to fix hallucinations.

statement.excerpt: much of what makes them scary is the assumption that OpenAI will fix hallucinations, something that the company has categorically failed to do.

from_speaker: something that the company has categorically failed to do
our_interpretation: Plain reading: as of the post, OpenAI had not stopped its models from hallucinating. They still made up facts at rates that matter in practice, as shown by OpenAI's own statements or published evaluations.
'Categorically failed' is read as 'has not fixed', not as 'made no progress at all'. Partial reduction does not contradict the claim unless hallucinations were close to eliminated.
Target period: from ChatGPT's launch (2022-11-30) to the post date. This is the record of OpenAI's efforts that the claim refers to.
criteria.support_condition: OpenAI's own documentation or independent evaluations from the period show its models still hallucinated in meaningful ways.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence from the period shows OpenAI's models had eliminated or nearly eliminated hallucinations.
